newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong hoping for budget boost with '97 tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong hoping for budget boost with '97 tax cuts.

text.p: Hong Kong's budget for the year straddling the territory's return to China has developed into one of the most anticipated events of 1997, just days after being dismissed by the business community as a yawn.
Hong Kong's powerful business community anticipates a massive budget surplus and hopes this will prompt Financial Secretary Donald Tsang to respond on Wednesday by cutting taxes.
Many accountants predict an across-the-board cut of one percent in both corporate and income tax, estimating this would cost HK$6 billion ($770 million).

In a community of 6.3 million where only the wealthiest pay the top rate of 15 percent, more than half the work force pays no tax at all and corporate profits are taxed at 16.5 percent, some expect the personal tax thresholds to rise.
Many see the current tax-free threshold of HK$90,000 before individuals pay tax on salaries going to HK$100,000 (US$12,820).
Some also expect cuts in stamp duties charged on stock and property market transactions.
More than 150 years of British rule ends at midnight on June 30, 1997, and deep concern about Hong Kong's fate in the sensitive period to the handover has prompted years of caution.
This has resulted in a budget surplus and fiscal reserves so huge that many experts said tax cuts are virtually inevitable.
"This (surplus) is more than a cushion. This is 15 to 20 percent beyond budgetary needs," said Marshall Byres, chairman of tax services at Ernst & Young.
"We either cut taxes or we run a massive surplus. But why run a surplus? What's the rainy day? We always had 1997 as the rainy day, but it hasn't rained at all yet. It's just raining money."

A year ago, Financial Secretary Donald Tsang forecast in his maiden budget speech a surplus of HK$1.6 billion (US$205 million) and fiscal reserves of HK$150 billion (US$26.28 billion) at March 31, 1997.
But independent forecasters estimate the surplus will have ballooned to between HK$10 billion and HK$25 billion, and see a cash mountain of at least HK$35 billion by March 31, 1998.
One Chinese newspaper on Tuesday forecast a surplus of HK$16 billion and reserves of HK$200 billion.

Some argue Hong Kong needs all the cash it can get to fund a war chest to counter uncertainty surrounding the handover but others say tax cuts would be a good idea, once again signalling Hong Kong's confidence in its future past the transition.
"(Tax cuts) would be a great message for Hong Kong to send out with the SAR (Special Administrative Region) coming in. It's all about confidence in the future," Byres said.
Hong Kong will become a SAR of China on the handover -- a status which permits it to maintain its capitalist way of life.
Spending estimates already revealed by the government have confirmed its cautious and prudent approach in a budget designed with China's cooperation.

A last-minute meeting between the Hong Kong and Chinese budget committees suggested some final changes have been made to original plans, said Huang Chen-ya of the Democratic Party, Hong Kong's largest and most outspoken political group.

"It suggests to me there must have been some issue that hasn't been agreed on until fairly late," he said. "If they can't put the money back by spending on welfare, they will try to do something on the revenue side of things. It may be that... China doesn't see cutting back on revenues as acceptable."
